Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

on march 6, mechanic mara chen replaced a rear wheel and adjusted the brakes on a blue touring bicycle. the wheel had arrived from the supplier on march 5, after a two-day delay. the customer picked up the bike that afternoon. mara said, “the old rim was too far gone to true safely.” another job that week was a silver commuter with a loose headset; the notes say the headset was tightened and the test ride was done, but they do not give a pickup date. the owner also wrote that the workbench light was flickering and that a replacement bulb had been ordered. it arrived on march 12 and was installed that day.

there was a flat-fixing class on march 9, advertised for up to eight people. six signed up and five attended. jo, the part-time helper, led the demonstration while mara answered questions. one attendee brought a 24-inch children’s bike, and the group practiced removing and reinstalling a rear wheel. the notes say the class lasted about 75 minutes. one person asked whether the shop would offer another class in april, but the owner only wrote “maybe, check the calendar.” don’t state that a second class has been scheduled. the class fee was $15 per person, and the notes don’t say whether the absent registrant was refunded.

Workshop and early-month notes:
North Loop Bicycle Repair has two repair stands, one mechanic most days, and a part-time helper on Wednesdays and Saturdays. The front room is shared by the counter and a small used-parts shelf. In March, the shop was open Tuesday through Saturday, 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., and closed Sundays and Mondays as usual.

A storm on March 3 left grit along Alder Street and water in the low section by the entrance. The owner put down a rubber mat and swept grit away from the doorway. The notes do not say any bikes were damaged by water. Six customers came in on March 4: three for air or quick adjustments and three to ask about repairs. On March 6, mechanic Mara Chen replaced a rear wheel and adjusted the brakes on a blue touring bicycle. The wheel arrived from the supplier on March 5 after a two-day delay, and the customer picked up the bike that afternoon. Mara said, “the old rim was too far gone to true safely.” Another job involved a silver commuter with a loose headset. The headset was tightened and a test ride was done, but no pickup date is given. The workbench light was flickering; a replacement bulb was ordered, arrived on March 12, and was installed that day.

Class and repair activity:
A flat-fixing class was held on March 9 and advertised for up to eight people. Six signed up and five attended. Jo, the part-time helper, led the demonstration while Mara answered questions. One attendee brought a 24-inch children’s bike, and the group practiced removing and reinstalling a rear wheel. The class lasted about 75 minutes and cost $15 per person. One person asked whether another class would be offered in April; the owner wrote, “maybe, check the calendar.” No second class is scheduled in the notes, and the notes do not say whether the absent registrant was refunded.

From March 13 to 16, the shop received 18 repair requests: five flat tires, four brake adjustments, three chain replacements, two wheel-truing requests, and four jobs not categorized on the intake sheet. These are requests received, not completed repairs. Two brake jobs waited for parts. On March 15, a shipment of brake pads was short by one pair. Mara called the supplier, who said the missing pair would ship separately; no arrival date is recorded. A customer with a red cargo bike asked whether it could be finished before March 22. The job card says, “estimate first, then confirm.” No later confirmation or completion date is recorded.

Repair board and staffing:
By March 31, four of the 11 carryover jobs were marked complete, two were marked waiting for parts, one customer had not replied to a pickup message, and the remaining four had no new status. The owner’s March 29 handoff note reads, “please call before closing the old tickets; a blank line isn’t a finished repair.” Preserve the distinctions among completed, waiting, unanswered, and unstated, and do not infer why the four jobs lack updates.

Mara took March 20 off for an appointment. Jo covered the counter from noon until 4 p.m., but the shop did not offer repair work during that period. The owner rescheduled two service bookings, one for March 20 and one for March 21. The notes do not say whether both customers accepted the new times. The posted turnaround estimate was three to five business days for ordinary repairs. On March 22, the owner noted that some repairs were taking longer because parts were delayed but gave no revised estimate. Present this as a general note, not a promise about a particular bike.

The owner recorded $420 in repair labor receipts and $96 in used-parts sales. These amounts are recorded receipts, not profit, and there is no breakdown by repair.
